translations.text: It is the custom of God's providence to instruct the minds of his creatures. So it was with Joseph and all the patriarchs: each of them was tested in measure with our strength.
As Job says: "Blessed is the man whom the Lord has reproved; do not reject the instruction of the Almighty, for he wounds and then heals again."
And Solomon says: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for trials."
And again: "The sons whom the Lord loves, he instructs and chastises." And the apostle says:

"Solid food is for the perfect," that is, for those who have been made worthy to receive the Lord's instruction with thanksgiving, and [in whom] his power is shown through the wrath of his indignation at sin [?].
He has endured with righteous long-suffering before repaying the lawless according to their wickedness, as David says:
"Be exalted, O judge of righteousness, and render recompense to the proud." And Paul says:

"Because of this the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience," as at the beginning of creation, in the days of Noah, at the destruction of proud men who had been created in the image of God.
Those ungrateful generations did not learn their own constitution and did not understand that they bore the likeness of his dominion. They despised the image of God the Creator,
They were humbled and became like that defeated nature of women, through whose disobedience death came in, as Paul says:
"Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived." And sin gave birth to those mixed offspring; by that excessive and shameless sin they angered God and made him repent of having made man.
His incomprehensible mercy could not endure it. For this reason he opened the floodgates of the waters and destroyed everyone in the flood.
But through blessed Noah a seed of inheritance was left for the world. Likewise, those plants of the curse, seeds of bitterness,
[we] recall: the abominable Sodomites in the time of righteous Lot, with their lawless intercourse. They left no room for mercy,
and upon them God rained fire and brimstone, and they were wiped out by that most extreme evil of destruction.
And again, that hideous woman Jezebel went beyond all bounds in lawlessness. Because of this Elijah was moved by divine zeal to shut the heavens, and he brought famine upon Israel,
just as Eve brought death into the world. On account of this Elijah says: "What have I to do with this house of Ahab?"
Because of Jezebel's disobedience, [Israel] reaped that fruit of drought.
For this reason he was handed over to an evil death, and his flesh was torn apart by the hooves of horses, and in him that scripture was fulfilled which says:
"Wrath kills the foolish man." But since drowning by water had been sealed off, and burning by fire had fallen from above,
from then on the sword was appointed by God to take vengeance on the wickedness of men, as Isaiah says:
"If you listen to me," he says, "you shall eat the good things of the land; if you do not listen, the sword shall devour you."
And remember briefly the trials that befell Israel from time to time when it turned toward sin, as David said:
"I remembered the days of old, and I spoke of all your commandments,"
so that, by remembering those earlier deeds, those who have knowledge may revere God's judgment, past and future, and both patterns, of good and of evil, may be told to the generations to come,
so that they might be found tested by other calamities, as Moses said:
"I will set a blessing upon you for good," for by those faithful ones who preach from God, taught by those who speak through the Holy Spirit, [?]
God is proclaimed a righteous judge: toward the vessels of mercy and sweetness, and with severity toward the fallen,
so that when the true worshippers of God see the fruit of righteousness, which is mercy,
they may trust in God and wait patiently to receive their reward; and again, so that when the false hear of the judgment of righteousness,
they may fear God's punishment, give up wickedness and hurry to repentance, like the Ninevites, and be saved from the ruin of soul and body.
In the same way the great house of Armenia sinned wickedly, as the prophet Jeremiah said in his Lamentations:

"With words of blasphemy they grieved the Holy Spirit, and with filthy deeds they angered their Creator beyond measure. Because of this, the wrath of God came to rest upon them in proportion to their lawlessness."
And he handed them over to the evil sword, to miserable captivity, to the twisting pain of hunger, and to the merciless slaughter of death, and there was no one to bury them.
And they fell to the ground like trees, as the prophet Isaiah says: "Unless the Lord of all [?]".
"It would have been better for them if they had [not?] known the way of truth, rather than knowing it and then turning back again."
For they cast away the orthodox faith of the holy catholic Church preached by the apostles, and they despised the church canon laid down by the teachers at the holy, God-inspired councils.
Therefore the root of bitterness was planted among them, the tares of wickedness sprang up, the sin of heresy grew, and the fruit of perdition multiplied upon them.
For the land of Armenia is arrogant, and its inhabitants are vainly boastful, greedy, insolent, sin-loving, proud, merciless,
loveless and full of every wickedness. Not one person was found in it who would bow his head to Christ; for them Christ died in vain.
And these are its boundaries and the names of its districts: Vanand, Ashornia, Bagrevand, Apahunik, Tsalkoitni, Chakat, Kogovit (two districts), Sharur,
Vaspurakan (twelve districts), Vayots Dzor (four districts), Dvinadasht (three districts), Gelakunia (four districts), Siunik (ten districts), Tashir and Kilbopori [?].
These eighty-seven districts were laid waste before the face of the Lord because of the evil of their sins, for in these districts there was not found a see of orthodox bishops,
nor the monastery of the orthodox, believing monks, as Abraham asks God:
"If there are five righteous, will you destroy that city?" And the Lord said, "No."
And it says: "Who that was holy ever perished, or where were the true uprooted root and all?"
Or where does it speak according to the word that God spoke to Eli: "Yet I will not destroy every man of yours from my altar,
so that he may see it and waste away, and so that these too may see it and waste away"?
The Lord set himself against these lands in the wrath of his anger, and by God's permission a Saracen king named Abul-Kasim was stirred up,
the son of the emir Abul-Saj and lord of Persia, who was served by sixty great cities and obeyed by seven powerful kings.
He armed himself with a great host and with chosen Kaets [?], of whom he had thousands and tens of thousands.
He entered the city of Dvin, and the groan of his wrath foretold the devastation of Armenia, as the destruction of the Ninevites had once been foretold, so that these too might repent.
But their hearts had been hardened like bronze and made fixed like the firmament,
for the sin of their change of faith was written "on a tablet of iron with a point of adamant," as Jeremiah says. For this reason they could not turn back.
For that house of Armenia became like the foolish man who built on a foundation of error and on the sand of heresy, and when the assaults arose,
"it fell, and great was its fall." As Job says:
"I have seen the foolish, whose roots had not spread, but suddenly their sustenance was devoured and their sons were removed far from life."
for their oppression, and the long-suffering of their authority [?], drained away their strength.
For this is their custom: first they demanded the tributes owed, and gifts and presents for their Kaets, for they were tributaries to him.
Then they asked for levies ahead of time. And they speak of their own impoverishment [?] as mere news [?], and hasten their own ruin.
And so by these schemes he emptied them of their wealth, so that he might easily become their master, and so it came to pass.
And when the Saracen was prevailing, and the king of the Armenians found no means of resistance, nor of escape,
for God had torn his kingdom from him, he then fled to the mountains of Abkhazia. In the end he did not escape death.
But that ruler pursued him with great fury, seeking to bring on him the punishment of death.
And they came to the fortress of Kveli, which belonged to Gurgen, eristav of eristavs. In it were noble aznaurs, and with them the blessed martyr of Christ, Gobron.
They came and besieged the fortress of Kveli. They pitched their tents all around it, like snow, and these barely fit, tightly crowded, within the bounds of five villages.
And the ropes of their tents were interwoven with one another, for this was the custom of their encampment, of those loathsome, godless peoples,
it was quickly set up [?]. They eat dogs, mice, human beings, and every unclean thing. And so they prepared for battle with many siege engines.
And the multitude of the arrows they shot blotted out the sunlight, for he had a hundred camel-loads of arrows alone, and the same of javelins.
And in that fierce battle the defenders of the fortress showed courage. They slew the attackers and threw their bodies to the ground like dung,
but the blessed Gobron was found foremost of all in courage, and the might of his fighting became known throughout that whole multitude.
And he changed his name, as all the saints did, as Peter was named Rock and Saul was named Paul.
He was first called Michael and afterwards Gobron. The king [?] had heard this and learned the name Gobron, and he marvelled at its sound and inscribed it on his heart,
for in his strong love for Gobron's fighting and valour, he grew zealous [?] against the Christian faith that Gobron held.
And whenever those multitudes poured out over the border of Artaani, and those whom they found gathering for themselves and reaping their fields [?],
Those who, because of hunger, disregarded the fear of death, they would gather near that fortress like sheep, as a spectacle for those inside, and cut their flesh to pieces.
And that innocent blood was offered to God like a fragrant sacrifice, like the blood of righteous Abel; their number God alone knows.
And countless multitudes of the Orthodox were shut up in Ajara and Shavsheti, and like locusts they ate the leaves of the trees and the green plants of the earth.
At that time Shavsheti became a fold that beasts could not enter, for such great numbers of those peoples, more than the land could hold, were standing nearby, only about half a day's journey away.
God did not allow them to go down into it, through the grace of the glorious deserts and the prayers of the saints,
whose good virtues are made firm like the pillars of heaven, and they stood against them like the walls of Raphat [?].
Now that ruler fought against that fortress for twenty-eight days, and the sappers [?] attacked it; they bored through the rock and breached the wall.
Blessed Gobron would sally out against them and drive them off, and by that victory he amazed everyone all the more.
And since there was no help and no way to resist, they asked for an oath, for God had given them up [?].
So he brought them out and separated from his own [?] about two hundred of them in number.
And he ordered that blessed Gobron be guarded more carefully than all the others, and so he set out.

And on the way he threatened some and promised them death, and to others he sent messengers and promised them good things, and in this way he tried to force them to be circumcised and to abandon Christ.

But blessed Gobron had nailed his flesh to the fear of God and had prepared himself for torments for Christ's sake and to endure death, as Christ endured death for all. And he spoke to them the words of the apostle:
"For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." And they reached Talin. And how much innocent blood was shed by them, who could count?
And that king, Smbat, went back again to his own land after the martyrdom of Saint Gobron.
As he could find no other way, he went into the fortress of Kapoeti. He was said to be the wisest of all the men of that time,
but since the help of God had left him, all his resources failed, and like an inexperienced man he shut himself in, and many people with him.
In the same way he besieged that fortress too, and after much fighting he took it, and he took captive all the princes, the great men of Armenia, and the nobles.
And after much torture he killed that king, and once he was beheaded, he hung him on a beam in the middle of the city of Dvin.
If one of the ignorant should speak about the divine judgments, those who know neither the teaching of the Scriptures nor the power of God,
and ask how these Christless, lawless nations have taken hold of such great might of dominion and such breadth of luxury,
or whether some possession of hope, or God's long-suffering, has taken it upon itself to bear with them — let there be no such thought! But as Paul says:
"What fellowship has light with darkness, or what agreement has Belial with Christ, or what part has an unbeliever with a believer?" And the Lord says:
"Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."
"And unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will have no life in yourselves." And again:
"Whoever disobeys the Son does not believe the Father either; he will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
So where can those lost ones find hope of salvation for their souls? For them the word of the cross is foolishness, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.
And Isaiah says: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
This mystery of salvation was prepared by the wisdom of the Creator for the flocks of Christ and the churches of God.
Think of sheep. If someone has many of them, does he not also get dogs to guard them, so that they are never slaughtered by wolves?
In the same way, these men stand around the sheep of Christ like fierce dogs, as their guardians. And Jerusalem, the holy city of the great King, of which Moses said:
"The eyes of the Lord are upon it always, from the beginning and forever," was built in the midst of vast deserts.
In those deserts live men of a beastlike nature, robbers, whose home and whose life is the back of a camel,
countless tribes. Against them these men are like dogs fighting those wild beasts, so that the churches of God may remain in peace.
Many evils [come?] upon these men [?], while the flocks of Christ learn in tranquility the service of God and not war, as the prophet says:
"They shall beat their swords into sickles and their spears into ploughshares," and they shall no longer learn war,
Just as now it is not at all fitting for Christians to [?] the sword among them, nor for a horseman to mount a horse. And after this Isaiah says:
"Then wolves will graze with lambs, and the leopard will lie down to rest with the kids; the calf and the bull and the lion will graze together."
By the wolf and the leopard he means the fury of their wickedness, which is like a beast's, quick to shed blood.
By the lion he means their tyranny and their rule. He speaks in terms of Daniel's vision of the beasts.
By the bear he means the kingdom of the Persians in Babylon, and by the lion the kingdom of the Saracens in Baghdad of Babylon. By the kid he means the heretics,
who appear meek on the outside but inside are wolves. As the Lord said: "Then he will set the kids on his left, and he will say to them:
'Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his servants.'" By the lamb he means the true flocks of Christ.
By the calf he means innocence. The bull is one of the clean animals, and its goring is the victory of the cross over its enemies.

And the two horns are faith made perfect by good works, like the two knives of the Gospel. Noah too foreshadowed the faith of the Church by bringing into the ark seven each of the clean animals and two each of the unclean.
But now, by the grace of God, the number of those who believe in Christ has spread a hundredfold, and [the beasts] do not harm them.
The lions and wolves have no power to tear apart the lambs of Christ's flocks, who graze together in peace.
And when that time arrived, a command went out from the ruler to summon those appointed to the table of martyrdom and to bring them before the [?] that terrible sentence of death,
as on that day of the Lord's judgment. Terrible and dreadful is that day of punishment, the second coming of the Lord, when the heavens will collapse and the orders of things will be changed,

all the luminaries will be extinguished and the earth will be shattered, the roar of the trumpet will strike terror into all created things, and with trembling they will behold Christ the King coming with the cross.
And although this is true, it is still something to be awaited by faith alone, as Paul says.
Faith is of great power, the proof of things not seen. Yet to human nature what is seen is reckoned more credible than what is told, and among visible things the terrible one is
the stroke of lightning, which is harsh, and even this, when it strikes [?], swiftly snatches away whatever is exposed [?] to it.
But for a man living in the flesh, nothing can be imagined more terrible or harsher than this: that a man, naked and condemned to death, should be led by the hand before countless merciless crowds
armed with drawn swords and levelled spears, with arrows held ready and knives prepared,
while he has a way of escape, and yet he endures it for the love of Christ, as the blessed Gobron endured.
For this was the custom of the Saracens. Whenever a command went out to kill a Christian,
they would arm themselves as on a day of battle, raise a [?] war-cry, and sharpen their swords to shed blood quickly, and they would race one another as if hurrying to gain great wealth.
And when they brought out those prisoners whom they had brought out of the fortress of Kveli, those whom God had chosen as his martyrs,
about one hundred and thirty-three in number, just as through Samuel God was pleased to make David his anointed,
the distinguished nobles were set apart in the same way, those whom King Adarnase ransomed.
And at that summons the saints understood what was about to happen, and all said together: "Let us go [?], brothers, with Christ, and let none of you waver."
And they came out with joy, and with cheerful faces they encouraged one another toward that harsh torment of death as though toward a good delight.
Most of them were brought before those terrible troops, who were ready with swords of every kind.
Then, like evil and enraged wild beasts, they fell upon them in confusion and raced one another; some struck them with swords,
some pierced them with spears and arrows and cut their flesh, slashed them apart with knives, and their livers were torn out as if by the mouths of dogs,
and so they shed their blood, and so their martyrdom was completed through Christ. But the blessed Gobron they brought before the emir.
And the emir said to the blessed Gobron: "I pity the beauty of your youth, and I grudge your knighthood to death, for you are renowned in our presence. And now,
as to a beloved son, I give you this counsel: abandon the faith of your folly, which did your companions no good, and confess the true faith of our dominion,
to which all things are subject. And I promise you, we know [?], that after this light thing, the rule of whatever [?] you wish,
I will give you a palace, tents, slaves, a mansion, camels and a great many fine goods, and I will make you one of my chosen men.
You will be dear to me and honored above all these troops."
The holy Gobron answered the emir and said to him: "I beg you, sovereign, do not force me to abandon Christianity,
in which my parents raised me, and with which I am sealed by the Holy Spirit. And what reason is this, that it should be a reason for my death?
There are many Christians under you, and I too will not fall short in serving your sovereignty in any way you may wish.
And know this for certain: neither by your good promises nor by bringing your many evil torments upon me will you be able to separate me from my Lord Jesus Christ."
Then the emir said to his servants: "Take him away and show him his slain companions, cut to pieces in various ways, and then show him the palaces and the tents,
and assure him that they will be given to him. Who knows? Perhaps fear of death or the good things to be gained will bend his heart."
When they had taken him around to all of it and had come back before the emir, the emir said: "What have you chosen for yourself?"
The holy Gobron said to him: "I told you from the very first that I will not turn away from Christ my Lord."
Then the emir said to his servants: "He does not know the pain of death. Take him away and kill the remaining Christians in front of him, and wound him a little, and then bring him back."
And again they took the blessed Gobron away. They set him among his remaining companions and fell upon them with swords without mercy.
As they struck them pitilessly, their blood spattered on him. One body would fall in front of him, and another body would roll under his feet.
And so the martyrdoms of all of them were carried out with terror, but they could not make his heart tremble.
They stretched out his neck and struck him with the sword just twice, and wounded him slightly.
The blessed man drew his hand out of his bonds, traced his own blood in the shape of a cross on his forehead, and said:
"I thank you, Lord Jesus Christ, who have made me worthy, unworthy sinner that I am and the last of all, of this share in the inheritance and in martyrdom.
"O Lord, bring to completion your mercy and your sweetness toward me, and let nothing at all make me stumble, neither any cause, nor the schemes and tyranny of this lawless one."
And again they brought him before the emir, and his face and his forehead shone brightly. And some of the Christians who were nearby
saw him with the eye of faith as one crowned from above, and they truly believed in his martyrdom.
And so he was adorned by the blood traced on his forehead, just as
when our Lord was undergoing his life-giving Passion and they led him out with the crown of thorns, and all saw him.
And it is about such a likeness that the Lord says: "It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher and his lord."
Then King Adarnase bore witness to his true martyrdom, like that of George and Theodore.
And when they presented him before the emir, the emir could not persuade him to abandon Christ, though he used many flattering words, and he said to him:
"Know this: if you do not turn and obey me, there is no way you will escape death."
So now listen to me, as to one who gives good counsel, and do not destroy yourself,
and I will order a physician to heal you of that small wound, and I will confirm for you the promises I made before."
Saint Gobron said to him: "Do whatever you wish. I am a Christian, and I will never deny his name."
Then the emir ordered that Saint Gobron be killed. They led him away and cut off his head, and threw him down among those who had been killed.
So his martyrdom was completed on the 17th of the month of November. He attained the unfading crown together with the holy apostles and all the martyrs.
Once again the Church put on the adornment of joy and splendour through his blood, and set on herself a crown of beauty and glory through his courage.
None of the Christians dared to approach him.
The emir ordered three pits to be dug. They gathered the bodies of all those who had been killed and threw them into them.
He also ordered that none of the Christians should approach them.
But God, who did not neglect his servants, glorified those who praised him and showed signs from above:
bright, shining lights all through the night, like burning lamps, which would stand over that pit.
Many people, believers and unbelievers alike, saw this sign. They came and told the emir.
But he gave an excuse, saying: "This also happens over the Saracens who are killed by the Greeks."
Now, beloved, let us obey the word of the apostle, share in the commemoration of the saints, and celebrate their memorial!
Just as the holy martyrs offered their souls to God through the torments of their bodies, are you not also able to offer such a sacrifice before God?
For although today there is no one who will cut your flesh with a sword for martyrdom, you are able to burn it away with hardship, sorrow and voluntary poverty for the Lord's sake.
This is the one who, though he could have [?] the delights and comforts of the world, freely chooses sorrow and hardship in their place.
He is the one who offers a sacrifice of praise before God, as did Gobron, the martyr of Christ.
Now therefore put your flesh to death and crucify it through toil and fasting, with the crown of the martyrs, for which the tyrants slaughtered the martyrs and they were martyred.
But you of your own will slay yourself through affliction. And this is a spotless sacrifice, which needs no priest to offer it, for whoever humbles himself on this earth,
will be exalted in heaven through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory with the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
